Okay, Diego, your article. Read us the key sentence from the abstract.
Patients treated with the new cream for twelve weeks had fewer flares than patients receiving a placebo.
Good. Now open it for us. Who are the two groups?
The patients who were treated with the cream, and the patients who were receiving a placebo. They were randomized at the start.
And is the efficacy real, or is the study underpowered?
It has three hundred participants enrolled in four centers, so the result looks robust.
Any caveat?
Yes. Notably, forty participants withdrew, and the authors don’t account for them in the main analysis.
Good catch. So, would you prescribe it on Monday?
Not yet. I’d wait for a second trial conducted by an independent group.

Every month I run the journal club for our dermatology residents, and the first thing I teach them is how to read one long sentence. Take this one: Patients treated with the new cream for twelve weeks showed fewer flares than patients receiving a placebo. It looks difficult, but it is two short sentences hidden inside one. The patients were treated with the new cream. The other patients were receiving a placebo. Authors remove the words who were, because journals have a word limit. So when you see a past participle like treated, enrolled or published right after a noun, read it as who were treated, or which was published. When you see an ing word like receiving or using, read it as who received, or who used. Once you can open a sentence like that, the article becomes much shorter. And then you can ask the real questions. How many participants were there? How many withdrew? Is the study robust, or is it underpowered?

In my first journal club in the United States, I presented a study about a topical treatment for acne, and I made one mistake that I will never forget. The abstract said: Participants using the gel twice a day improved more than participants using it once a day. I read it too fast, and I told everybody that the gel was better than the placebo. My attending stopped me, very politely. She said: read the sentence again. Who is being compared with whom? Of course, there was no placebo group in that sentence at all. Both groups were using the gel. The study compared two doses, not the gel and a placebo. Since then, I always do the same thing before I speak. I open every long sentence, I find the two groups, and I say the comparison in my own simple words. It takes thirty seconds, and it has saved me from a lot of embarrassing moments.

This study, published last year, looked at a new topical cream. Patients enrolled in the trial were randomized into two groups. Patients receiving the cream improved more than patients receiving a placebo. Notably, the effect was larger in patients treated for more than eight weeks. However, many participants withdrew before the end, so the study may be underpowered. In my opinion, the result is interesting, but we need a larger trial.
